edges.relationship: Erickson compares Clark’s three forms of household production with the family economy categories used jointly by Louise Tilly and Joan Scott.
edges.evidence_note: Erickson’s 1992 introduction ix explicitly aligns Clark’s domestic, family and capitalistic industry with Tilly and Scott’s 1978 family economy, family wage economy and family consumer economy terminology. The comparison is the named scholar’s account, not proof of direct transmission or identical chronology. Louise Tilly’s equal credit is retained; she has no full endpoint and is distinct from Charles Tilly. Erickson immediately questions Clark’s chronology and the conflation of capitalism with mechanization. Clark’s own introduction 6–8 says the forms overlap and coexist rather than succeeding along hard boundaries. Original Tilly–Scott 1978 book and the complete Clark book remain unread.

edges.relationship: Labrousse identifies an economic rereading of Marx, equipped by Simiand and Aftalion’s methods and checked against historical evidence, as a formative resource.
edges.evidence_note: Own interview 112–113 explicitly describes his methodological relationship to Simiand, says he never followed Simiand’s teaching, and credits Simiand and Aftalion with instruments for rereading Marx from 1925. Their roles and the historical control are integral, not Marx as sole source or a direct teacher. He acknowledges only indirect Durkheim exposure. Own 123 rejects automatic economic causation and an absolute impoverishment thesis he calls unfaithful to Marxism; this is not blanket doctrinal agreement. Interviews recorded late 1978/early 1979 and published 1980; original Marx works and private seminar records remain unread.

edges.relationship: Labrousse takes up Febvre’s economies, societies and civilizations formula to explain a program of interrelated collective forces and changing research priorities.
edges.evidence_note: Own Annales answer 114 explicitly attributes the three-term formula to Febvre, stresses their interrelations and shifting emphases rather than an unchanging hierarchy, and on 115 calls the triple watchword his operational strategy. This is a particular programmatic use, not formal supervision, invention of all social history or endorsement of every Febvre argument. His acknowledgment of individual agency and complementarity with cultural history remains. No complete Febvre text newly read.

edges.relationship: Labrousse invokes Braudel’s Mediterranean study as an exemplary account of collective forces shaping apparently freer political and individual history.
edges.evidence_note: Own 114 Annales answer singles out Braudel’s Philippe II as an enduring example while insisting that collective history need not suppress the individual. Charle’s note4 identifies La Méditerranée and its 1966 second edition, separately recording 1949 first publication. The exemplar supports a bounded conceptual resource, not proof of first-reading date, formal mentoring or equal rhythms for all historical forces. Original Braudel monograph remains unread. This incoming resource is distinct from the existing reverse Labrousse-to-Braudel contribution 445.

edges.relationship: Braudel questions Labrousse’s return toward short-duration revolutionary crises while praising his work and accepting the usefulness of connecting economic and political events.
edges.evidence_note: Actual original 1958 pages 730–731 contrast Labrousse’s 1933 secular price inquiry with the shorter revolutionary-crisis inquiry and especially Comment naissent les révolutions? 1948. Braudel calls the operation legitimate and useful but symptomatic of a return to short time, alongside exceptionally strong praise of La Crise. He also says social and economic conjunctures need not move at identical speeds. This is a particular temporal disagreement, not rejection of Labrousse’s research or an independently proved failure. Braudel’s 1943 dating is preserved as his printed wording; the graph’s separately established 1944 book publication is unchanged. Original Labrousse monographs and 1948 paper remain unread.

edges.relationship: Hill questions Yates’s explanation of Hermeticism’s displacement by mechanical philosophy and argues for greater weight on political fear of radicalism.
edges.evidence_note: Own complete 1973 review calls the supersession account less convincing, questions the explanatory weight of the 1659 Dee diary publication, and stresses social and political hostility to Rosicrucian radicalism. He also suggests her dynastic starting point may understate its radical associations. This is a scoped explanatory disagreement, partly developing hints he expressly credits Yates herself with supplying, alongside strong praise for her discoveries and future research possibilities. It does not reject her whole work or claim her original book has been newly read. The existing reverse Yates-to-Hill resource edge 506 remains exact.

edges.relationship: Brandon identifies James’s draft reading and intervention on slave resistance as concrete resources in Williams’s development of Capitalism and Slavery.
edges.evidence_note: Brandon 2017:317–319 and notes 57–71 reports repeated draft reading, the last-minute addition of The Slaves and Slavery, and Williams’s own bibliographical acknowledgment of The Black Jacobins. This is explicitly scholarly mediation through Brandon and his named historical witnesses, not a fresh reading of the original drafts, 1944 bibliographical page 268, James’s book or correspondence. Brandon distinguishes joint Padmore/James political resources, later political divergence and different emphases on enslaved self-activity versus conflicts within the capitalist class. James is a particular contributor, not the sole origin of every Williams thesis or proof of Williams’s Marxist affiliation.

edges.relationship: As Brandon recounts, James criticized the optimistic forecast for Caribbean development in Williams’s The Negro in the Caribbean while praising its historical analysis and democratic commitment.
edges.evidence_note: Brandon 2017:325–326 quotes James’s review objecting that the historical account of capitalism’s long operation did not justify a sudden hopeful change in its future behavior. The target is Williams’s 1942 book and its forecast, alongside praise for his history, nationalism and democracy; this is not a direct rejection of the 1944 Capitalism and Slavery or a verdict that all independence projects fail. Brandon’s note 97 identifies James’s W. F. Carlton pseudonym and the 1943 review. Original review and complete 1942 book remain unread; the criticism is explicitly mediated and does not erase the separate constructive scholarly relationship.
